entities.name: Titus Aurelius Fulvus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Titus Aurelius Fulvus, a distinguished Roman senator and military commander of the late 1st century CE, served as consul suffectus in 84 CE and held significant gubernatorial postings across the Roman Empire. His historical importance stems not only from his own accomplished career but profoundly from his direct lineage to one of Rome's most revered emperors: he was the paternal grandfather of Antoninus Pius, whose reign (138-161 CE) marked a period of unprecedented peace and stability known as the *Pax Romana*. Fulvus's career trajectory under Emperors Vespasian, Titus, and Domitian exemplifies the opportunities for advancement within the burgeoning imperial bureaucracy for men of senatorial rank.

Beginning his public life during the Flavian dynasty, Fulvus likely held a series of military tribuneships and quaestorships, common for men of his station. His first major appointment was as governor of Hispania Tarraconensis around 70-73 CE, a crucial province in western Rome known for its mineral wealth and strategic importance. Subsequently, he achieved the prestigious office of consul suffectus in 84 CE, a testament to his political influence and the favor of Emperor Domitian. Later, he served as the proconsul of Asia around 92-93 CE, governing one of the wealthiest and most culturally significant provinces in the eastern Mediterranean.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Titus Aurelius Fulvus was a significant figure in Roman administration and politics, whose distinguished career as consul and governor provided the foundational prestige for his family, directly contributing to his grandson Antoninus Pius becoming emperor during the Pax Romana.
